```
$ rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'
```

Instead of writing out the glob every time, you can use ripgrep's support for
file types:

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
```

or, more succinctly,

```
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

The way the `--type` flag functions is simple. It acts as a name that is
assigned to one or more globs that match the relevant files. This lets you
write a single type that might encompass a broad range of file extensions. For
example, if you wanted to search C files, you'd have to check both C source
files and C header files:

```
$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
```

or you could just use the C file type:

```
$ rg 'int main' -tc
```

Just as you can write blacklist globs, you can blacklist file types too:

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
```

or, more succinctly,

```
$ rg clap -Trust
```

That is, `-t` means "include files of this type" where as `-T` means "exclude
files of this type."

To see the globs that make up a type, run `rg --type-list`:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

By default, ripgrep comes with a bunch of pre-defined types. Generally, these
types correspond to well known public formats. But you can define your own
types as well. For example, perhaps you frequently search "web" files, which
consist of JavaScript, HTML and CSS:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

or, more succinctly,

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

The above command defines a new type, `web`, corresponding to the glob
`*.{html,css,js}`. It then applies the new filter with `-tweb` and searches for
the pattern `title`. If you ran

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' --type-list
```

Then you would see your `web` type show up in the list, even though it is not
part of ripgrep's built-in types.

It is important to stress here that the `--type-add` flag only applies to the
current command. It does not add a new file type and save it somewhere in a
persistent form. If you want a type to be available in every ripgrep command,
then you should either create a shell alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or add `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` to your ripgrep configuration file.
([Configuration files](#configuration-file) are covered in more detail later.)

#### The special `all` file type

A special option supported by the `--type` flag is `all`. `--type all` looks
for a match in any of the supported file types listed by `--type-list`,
including those added on the command line using `--type-add`. It's equivalent
to the command `rg --type agda --type asciidoc --type asm ...`, where `...`
stands for a list of `--type` flags for the rest of the types in `--type-list`.

As an example, let's suppose you have a shell script in your current directory,
`my-shell-script`, which includes a shell library, `my-shell-library.bash`.
Both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` would only search for matches in
`my-shell-library.bash`, not `my-shell-script`, because the globs matched
by the `sh` file type don't include files without an extension. On the
other hand, `rg --type-not all` would search `my-shell-script` but not
`my-shell-library.bash`.

{"command":"cat > <path> <<'EOF'
# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

A file type in ripgrep is just a name attached to one or more file name
patterns. `rust` means `*.rs`. `make` means `*.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile,
Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile`. That's the whole idea. The four
flags below let you use those names, list them, and define your own.

## See what you already have

Start here:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

Each line is a type name, a `:`, and then a comma-delimited list of the
patterns that make it up. ripgrep ships with more than 200 type names, so pipe
the output through ripgrep itself when you're looking for one:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

Some types have aliases. `py` and `python` are the same type, as are `md` and
`markdown`. `--type-list` also reflects any types you added or cleared in the
same command, which makes it the fastest way to check a definition you just
wrote.

## `-t/--type`: only these files

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

Both forms work; the short flag takes its value with no space. Pass the flag
more than once to search several types at once:

```
$ rg 'TODO' -trust -tmd
```

Naming a type that doesn't exist is an error, not a silent no-op:

```
$ rg -tnope title
rg: unrecognized file type: nope
```

## `-T/--type-not`: everything but these files

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

`-t` means "include files of this type", `-T` means "exclude files of this
type". You can mix them, and here order matters. When a file matches both an
included and an excluded type, the flag written later on the command line
wins:

```
$ rg --type-add 'foo:*.{rs,foo}' -tfoo -Trust title
main.foo:title

$ rg --type-add 'foo:*.{rs,foo}' -Trust -tfoo title
main.foo:title
main.rs:title
```

Note that type filters have lower precedence than the `-g/--glob` flag and
than any rules in your ignore files. If your `.gitignore` excludes a file,
`-t` won't bring it back.

## `--type-add`: define your own

The format is `name:glob`, and one glob per flag:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

A brace alternation gets you the same thing in one flag:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

By default, globs are added to whatever ripgrep already defines for that name,
so `--type-add 'md:*.markdown'` extends the built-in `md` type rather than
replacing it. Type names must consist only of Unicode letters or numbers —
`my-web` is rejected — and `all` is reserved.

You can also build a type out of other types with the include directive:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc title
```

Every name after `include:` must already be defined at the point the flag is
read, so put your `--type-add` definitions before any include that uses them.
If one name in the list is bad, the whole definition is rejected and nothing
changes. You can keep adding plain globs to an included type afterward:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' title
```

## What the globs match

Type globs are matched against the file name only, never the full path. So
`--type-add 'web:src/*.js'` will never match anything — use `-g` for path
patterns and save types for names. Types also don't apply to directories.

This is also why a file with no extension slips through most types. A shell
script named `my-shell-script` isn't matched by `-tsh`, because the `sh` globs
all require an extension.

## `--type-clear` and the `all` type

`--type-clear NAME` throws away the existing globs for a type, and you can add
new ones afterward. Order matters:

```
$ rg --type-clear md --type-add 'md:*.markdown' --type-list | rg '^md:'
md: *.markdown
```

Reverse those two flags and the clear wipes out your addition too.

Both `-t` and `-T` accept the special value `all`. `-tall` searches every file
matched by any defined type, custom types included — whitelist mode, where
ripgrep only searches files it recognizes. `-Tall` is the inverse: it searches
only the files no type recognizes. That's the fast way to find your
extensionless scripts, stray data dumps, and anything ripgrep doesn't have a
name for yet.

## Making a type stick

`--type-add` and `--type-clear` apply to the current command only. Nothing is
persisted. To get a type in every invocation, either alias it:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or put it in your configuration file, one argument per line:

```
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}
```

ripgrep reads that file from the path in `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH`, and it won't
look anywhere else. Once it's there, `-tweb` works everywhere, and
`--type-list` will show `web` alongside the built-ins.
